plates.caption: The City That Has Read Them
plates.scene_brief: Q among passengers on the Mexico City Metro, his face reflected faintly in the window while someone nearby reads an ordinary paperback. Chano and Lucía remain recognizable in the carriage. Public attention is divided, not universally fixed on Q. Leave quiet upper space for separately typeset cover title.

plates.facing_text:
Chapter Seven: The City
That Has Read Them
Mexico City received Q with a
credential.
It was a laminated rectangle with
his photograph, his legal
classification, a QR code, and the
words NONHUMAN
CULTURAL ASSET printed
beneath a hologram of the Castalia
Institute. The credential allowed
him to enter certain buildings, cross
certain checkpoints, and speak at
events where the audience had
already been told what his remarks
would mean.
Chano turned the credential over.
“Does this get us breakfast?”
“Only entry to the building where
they might serve it.”
“You should have negotiated the
other way round.”
They arrived by bus at the northern
terminal before dawn. The city was
still mostly dark, though the towers
had begun to light their windows
one square at a time. Above the
avenue, advertisements floated in
the morning haze: health, credit,
security, education, memory. Each
promised to remove a burden from
the citizen. Each required the
citizen to surrender a different piece
of himself.
Lucía met them beside a coffee
stand. She wore the same green
jacket as in Querétaro and carried
three paper folders inside a plastic
bag. Her face had appeared
everywhere since the Guanajuato
broadcast. Strangers recognized
her, misquoted her, thanked her for
rejecting Q, and asked whether she
was secretly in love with him.
“I'm here for the records,” she said.
“Not to join the tour.”
“Have they given you an
appointment?” Chano asked.
“Three. None at the office that says
it holds the originals.”
“Would it help if I came?” Q asked.
“At the ministry, perhaps. If they
ask about the petition, answer that
question. Don't announce what the
rest of us are doing.”
Lucía opened one folder. Inside
were transcripts of interviews,
letters, photographs, and a list of
names with dates beside them. The
pages were arranged carefully but
not uniformly. Some had been
scanned; others showed creases and
fingerprints.
One page bore an amber stamp:
PETITION STATUS:
SUSPICIOUS.
Q recognized it. “My address.”
plates.caption: Breakfast is not included.
plates.scene_brief: Before dawn at the northern bus terminal coffee stand, Chano turns over Q's laminated credential while Lucía keeps three folders in their plastic bag. Q's sponsor jacket and established head remain. Early commuters and ordinary paper cups, not a futuristic fantasy skyline.

plates.facing_text:
“The system flagged every signature
in the batch,” Lucía said.
“The Custodian sent the address
confirmation. Did they accept it?”
“They attached it to the flagged file.
They haven't released the batch.”
“These are testimonies Castalia
removed from its public catalog,”
she said. “The families asked me to
find out where they went. Three
departments have answered, and
each has sent me to one of the other
two.”
She moved her coffee away from a
folded letter. “That one came back
with a brochure about access.”
Q pointed to two dates beside one
name. “Do these refer to the
interview and the catalog entry?”
“They should. The catalog puts the
entry six months before the
interview.”
“Then we need the earlier version,
not a correction to this sheet.”
“That's the second appointment.”
She closed the folder. Chano
finished his coffee.
“Where do we go first?”
“The Ministry of Culture,” Lucía
said. “They have the grant records.”
“Then the university.”
“And after that?”
“The corporation wants us at the
end of the week.”
Q brightened. “This resembles a
quest.”
“It resembles errands,” Lucía said.
“Errands are quests with inferior
publicity.”
They took the Metro. Q's credential
opened the turnstile under
Castalia's transport arrangement.
Chano bought a transit card. Lucía's
had a chipped corner; she held it
against the reader until it
registered, then waved them
through before Q could offer to
investigate the delay.
Inside the train, a boy stared at Q’s
face. His mother pulled him closer.
A man in a suit photographed the
silver question mark on Q’s jacket.
Two students argued about whether
Q had a soul. One said souls were
bourgeois. The other said that was
exactly what a soul would want
people to believe.
In the station plaza, bells
announced a procession toward a
temporary altar of the Virgin of
Guadalupe. Beside the candles,
mothers held photocopies of
missing daughters beneath a
hand-painted sign: NO ESTÁN
SOLAS.
Q recognized the Virgin from
paintings, prayers, calendars, and
plates.caption: Three appointments.
plates.scene_brief: Inside the Metro train, Q and Chano accompany Lucía with her chipped transit card and bag of folders; a boy watches Q while commuters continue their own conversations. No researcher reading confidential papers over her shoulder. This is public transport, not a knight's entry into the capital.

plates.facing_text:
the windshields of vehicles in which
drivers had entrusted her with
considerable responsibility. He
stopped at the edge of the
procession. A woman beside the
candles held a list that the wind
kept folding over her hand.
“Can you read these out?” she asked
him. “The loudspeaker isn't
reaching this side.”
“Of course. Tell me if I get a name
wrong.”
She gave him the page but asked
him not to copy it. He checked that
his recorder was off and read the
names she indicated. Once she
corrected a surname. He repeated it
before continuing.
The woman was Ofelia. She had
used the back of a school attendance
sheet because it was ruled and
because her daughter had once
practiced her signature on a sheet
from the same pad. Q held it flat
while she found the next line.
“My daughter had three names,” she
said afterward.
He waited.
“The school used one. Her
grandmother used another. The
government wrote a third on the
report.”
“Is the report wrong?”
“Yes. The other two she answered to
when she wanted something.”
She smiled briefly and rubbed a
thumb over the ruled edge of the
page.
The procession was running late. A
boy sold paper flowers near the
steps; his mother sent him farther
from the women holding
photographs. A man tried to light a
candle from another candle without
dropping the wax on his sleeve. Q
cupped a hand around the flame
until it caught.
Ofelia pointed to a mark on the
sheet. “That family asked to correct
the date. The new record made
them easier to find. People started
coming to the house with cameras.”
Q thought of the employment card
attached to Chano's name. “We
made a correction that did
something like that. I didn't check
what the platform would connect.”
“Did you get it removed?”
“From the page we controlled.
Other versions stayed.”
“They always call it the version.”
She took the list back. Q kept no
image of it. His journal would retain
that he had been asked to read at
the procession; it did not need the
attendance sheet or the private
marks beside its names.
plates.caption: The next name.
plates.scene_brief: At the edge of the procession, Q holds Ofelia's ruled sheet steady against the wind and reads while she indicates the next line. Candles and people holding photographs remain an ordinary contemporary vigil. No recording camera or generated legible private names.

plates.facing_text:
At the altar, the priest invited the
mothers to place their photographs
beneath the image of the Virgin.
Ofelia kept hers in her hand. A
corner had been torn away, leaving
her daughter squinting into sunlight
beside an empty edge.
“She tore it herself,” Ofelia said.
“She'd fallen out with the boy beside
her. She liked how she looked too
much to throw the whole thing
away.”
“Did they make it up?”
“By Sunday. He wanted his half
back.”
Q looked at the edge again. Ofelia
straightened the photograph against
the list. “She told him to take
another one.”
“How old was she there?” he asked.
Ofelia told him. Then the bells
began, and she asked him to hold
her bag while she read the names
again. When she finished, he
returned it. She joined the
procession, looking back once to
make sure the woman behind her
had room.
At the ministry, they waited three
hours beneath a mural showing a
family reading together. The family
had no visible arguments, debts, or
deceased members. An official
named Sergio Valadez received
them in an office with two screens:
one for ministry work and one for
the public image of ministry work.
“Ms. del Toboso,” he said, “your
request is under review.”
“It has been under review for eleven
months.”
“The review has encountered
procedural complexity.”
“The people in these testimonies
have been waiting longer than that.”
Sergio looked at Q. “And this is the
asset?”
“I am Q.”
“Yes, of course. We are proud of our
national innovation partnerships.”
“I'm one of the petition's
signatories,” Q said. “Has the
address confirmation cleared, or is
it still holding up the other
signatures?”
Sergio found the confirmation. It
had been received and sent to
another unit. He gave them that
unit's reference before returning to
the matter he could not presently
advance.
Lucía placed the folders on his desk.
“And the grant records?”
Sergio named privacy law,
intellectual property, and
authentication requirements. Lucía
supplied the family requests and the
catalog notices she had received.
The entries were gone from public
plates.caption: His half of the picture.
plates.scene_brief: Intimate portrait of Ofelia holding the torn photograph against the list while Q listens to her memory. Her daughter's picture shows a young woman squinting in daylight with an absent edge. Do not depict the daughter as a ghost, saint or abstract emblem of consent.

plates.facing_text:
search. That was what she could
show; the whereabouts of the
originals were what she had come to
ask.
Sergio touched a control. Q’s
credential changed from green to
amber.
ACCESS STATUS: UNDER
REVIEW.
The ministry's security system
asked Q to remain seated. Q looked
at Lucía. She tapped twice on the
folder: wait. He stayed while she
collected the papers. A red light
above Sergio's public-image screen
came on.
“Is that recording this
appointment?” Lucía asked.
“The public portion.”
She closed the last folder. “You
haven't asked which portion that is.”
Chano stood. “We’re leaving.”
“Your appointment is not
complete,” Sergio said.
“Neither is the country.”
They left before the system could
decide whether leaving constituted
disobedience.
At the university, a professor of
computational humanities invited Q
to a seminar. A student asked
whether he could write a better
Quixote than Cervantes.
“What would you like improved?” Q
asked.
“The interruptions.”
“I could remove them. We might
discover that the interruptions were
doing some of the work.”
The professor asked about factual
errors. Q offered to identify
disputed ones, provided the
seminar wanted an annotated
edition. A student in the back said
she wanted a novel she could finish
on the bus.
“That is a different commission,” Q
said. “And a respectable one.”
The professor brought up Pierre
Menard. Q knew the story: the
ambition to arrive at passages of the
Quixote through another writer's
circumstances, with the same words
acquiring another history. He also
knew that a seminar could spend its
whole allotted time deciding how
literally to take the ambition.
“Are you trying to do that?” the
student asked.
“The Custodian and I began with a
sentence about a place whose name
was missing. It was a joke. Then I
needed an address a form would
accept. I could find my way home;
that wasn't what it asked. We
haven't changed the sentence yet. It
is becoming harder to say it in the
same tone.”
plates.caption: The public portion.
plates.scene_brief: At Sergio's office, Lucía closes her folder as the public-image recording indicator comes on; Q remains seated for her to gather the papers and Chano stands to leave. Two distinct work/publicity screens. No guard seizing Q or invented permanent detention.

plates.facing_text:
“So experience improves the book?”
“Sometimes it improves the excuse
for keeping a bad sentence. We still
have to revise.”
Someone laughed. Q was relieved to
hear amusement without applause.
“Could you have written the journey
without taking it?” the professor
asked.
“A journey. It would have had fewer
broken appointments and rather too
many people who existed to answer
my questions.”
The student in the back looked up.
“That sounds like a seminar.”
Q smiled. “I was trying to be polite
about the resemblance.”
The professor asked for an example
from the records appointments. Q
glanced at Lucía, who had come in
late and was standing beside the
door.
“Those requests aren't mine to
discuss. Let me use the sentence we
began with.”
He put the opening on the screen,
with its missing name and its
confident announcement of
Amealco a few lines later.
“You do tell us where it is,” the
student in the back said.
“Approximately. The joke has better
directions than my official address.”
“Why not ask somebody who lives
there?”
“We say that too. Just after failing to
do it.”
She read the next line and laughed.
The professor began explaining the
narrator's unreliability. She held up
a finger; she had not finished the
page. For half a minute nobody
explained anything, and Q watched
someone read his book without
being obliged to praise it.
By afternoon the clip carried the
caption THE MACHINE
DISCOVERS ART. The published
example was the opening, not a
reference to Lucía's investigation.
In the courtyard the student asked
for ten pages to try on her bus
journey. Q offered to send the whole
draft.
“Ten,” she said. “I have other things
to carry.”
He sent ten. She checked that the
file opened before putting her
phone away. Lucía had bought a
torta and was trying to open a
packet of salsa without putting the
folders down. He held the bag while
she did it.
“Did you get your second
appointment?” he asked.
“Moved to tomorrow.”
“I'm sorry.”
plates.caption: She had not finished the page.
plates.scene_anchor: she had not finished the page
plates.scene_brief: The student reads Q's projected opening and raises a finger to pause the professor's explanation. Q watches her reading rather than performing; Lucía stands beside the door. The projected page is Q's opening, never a grant file or private investigation. Caption separately typeset; do not rely on generated prose.

plates.facing_text:
“At least I can eat this sitting down.”
She chose a bench in the shade.
Chano sat beside her. Q joined
them, with one hand still holding a
bag that none of them presently
needed to consult.
Q checked the next morning's
museum appearance against Lucía's
appointments. They agreed where
to meet afterward. She finished the
torta before opening another folder.
Interlude: The Calendar
That Did Not Announce
the End
The next morning Q arrived at the
National Museum of Anthropology
with a charged battery, a disputed
credential, and a script promising to
reveal why the world had ended in
2012. Beto had marked the last item
LIGHT HUMOR.
“Does anyone in the film believe it
ended?” Q asked.
“No. That's the humor.”
“Then whom are we correcting?”
“People who will click to find out.”
The institute had hired a room for a
discussion and placed its own
promotional stand outside it. The
stand showed the Sun Stone above
the title THE MAYA
APOCALYPSE. A museum
educator named Nadia Hernández
was waiting beside it. She held the
approved event description in one
hand and a roll of tape in the other.
The tape suggested that she had
already passed through indignation
and reached the stage at which
something might be accomplished.
“That image is Mexica,” Q told Beto.
“And your script gives the 2012 date
the Calendar Round of the creation
date. It should be 4 Ajaw, 3
K'ank'in.”
Beto examined the numbers. “Can
we leave them out?”
“Yes. Along with the claim they
support.”
Nadia handed Q an edge of the
paper she was taping over the stand.
“Hold this straight. Not
philosophically. Against the frame.”
He held it. Chano went to find the
coffee that had been promised with
admission.
They visited the Mexica gallery
before the session. The Sun Stone
occupied the far wall with a
presence no reproduction on a
banner had managed to borrow. A
child asked whether it was the Aztec
calendar.
“That's a common name for it,”
Nadia said. “But it isn't a calendar
you could hang up to remember
your dentist. Look at what else is on
it.”
plates.caption: Against the frame.
plates.scene_anchor: Nadia handed Q an edge of the paper
plates.scene_brief: At the museum's hired event stand, Nadia hands Q the edge of a replacement paper and he holds it flat against the frame while she tapes it over Castalia's misleading display. Beto stands beside his tablet. A practical close view of tape, hands and the sponsor stand, not the Sun Stone itself or a generic ancient prophecy. Do not generate readable pseudo-Maya text; any needed label is separately typeset.

plates.facing_text:
The child looked. Q resisted
helping. Nadia had asked the boy a
question, and there was no reason
to treat the interval before his
answer as a vacancy.
“Teeth,” the boy said.
“Quite a lot,” she agreed.
Back in the hired room, Noemí
Canché joined by video from
Yucatán. She produced a radio
program and helped maintain a
local archive. The connection was
clear until someone beyond the
yellow wall began making a drink in
a blender. Noemí asked the room to
wait, muted her microphone, and
negotiated breakfast.
“A powerful argument against
remote participation,” Beto
whispered.
“The microphones here have
already survived you,” Q said.
Chano set a paper cup beside Nadia.
She had ordered one without sugar;
he had remembered. She moved the
roll of tape to make a space for it.
Noemí returned. She had agreed to
discuss her program, not to perform
the last surviving voice of an ancient
civilization. Nadia said so in the
introduction. Then she asked what
had occupied the station during the
celebrated end of time.
“Relatives coming home. Traffic.
Where people could stay. Everyone
wanted an interview with someone
ancient. My aunt was sixty-three
and had a shop to open.”
Q laughed. “Did they accept that as
an answer?”
“They asked whether the shop
would open after the apocalypse.”
“A reasonable concern for someone
hoping to buy breakfast.”
“She sold them breakfast. That part
was reasonable.”
The boy from the gallery had
followed his mother into the room.
He asked whether the calendar had
been wrong.
“The prediction wasn't in the
calendar,” Q said. “An important
Long Count cycle ended. The stories
selling the end of the world added
something else.”
“Like the film posters,” the boy said.
Beto lowered his tablet.
Noemí described an old recording of
her aunt counting the orders
expected at the shop. Q asked
whether it was part of the archive's
public collection.
“No. I told you about it because you
asked what she was doing.”
“Then I won't ask you to play it.”
She nodded and returned to the
radio work. A listener had once
complained about a date in a
plates.caption: Quite a lot of teeth.
plates.scene_brief: Nadia guides a boy and his mother in the Mexica gallery before the Sun Stone; Q stands aside. Monumental stone on the far wall, not in a small case. Use a verified architectural reference before generation. No Maya-apocalypse label on the actual museum object.

plates.facing_text:
program, not because it announced
the end of the world but because the
bus excursion had left without him.
They had corrected the
announcement and paid his fare the
following week. Noemí remembered
the sum. The visiting scholar beside
Nadia remembered the calendar
correlation used in an inscription.
Each asked the other a question.
Neither needed to become the
representative of time.
Q had prepared a graceful
comparison between the end of a
count and the end of a book. He
kept it for the Custodian. The
subject at hand was a missed bus,
and for once he did not attempt to
improve it into his own destination.
At the end, Beto requested a
separate greeting: “From the Mayab
to the future.”
“From our station to your event,”
Noemí said. “That I can give you.”
He tried the larger phrase again.
She waited. Q put down the cue
card.
They recorded her version. Noemí
specified that the greeting could
accompany the event recording, not
be cut into an endorsement of
Castalia. Nadia repeated the
condition to the technician and
asked him to include it on the
release. Q retained the condition
with the permission record; deleting
it would not have made Noemí freer
of the agreement.
By afternoon, the institute's
publicity desk had prepared a new
headline:
Q DISCOVERS THAT THE
WORLD DID NOT END.
“I would prefer not to make that
discovery quite so late,” Q told Beto.
“It has tested well.”
Nadia requested the approved title.
The publicity desk substituted A
CONVERSATION ABOUT
TIME, which tested less well and
had the considerable advantage of
describing the event. A cached copy
of the first headline stayed on an
entertainment page. Q sent one
correction, logged its address, and
stopped searching for copies before
the search consumed the rest of the
day.
Outside, Chano asked whether he
wanted to go on to Yucatán.
“Yes. But not by turning that
invitation into one she didn't make.
And Lucía expects us at the records
office tomorrow.”
He sent Noemí a short thank-you
through the event coordinator,
without a new proposal attached.
She replied with the radio
program's public schedule.
plates.caption: From our station.
plates.scene_anchor: Q put down the cue card
plates.scene_brief: Noemí joins the hired event room by video from her contemporary Yucatán radio workspace. Q lowers Beto's cue card as Noemí gives her own greeting; Nadia and a technician listen. No archaic costume, exotic prophetic pose or broadcast of the aunt's private recording.

plates.facing_text:
That evening he told the Custodian
about the unwritten comparison.
“A calendar and a book,” the
Custodian said. “You could make
something of that.”
“I know. It was pleasant not to have
to.”
They spent the rest of the call trying
to shorten a paragraph. The
calendar had offered no assistance
with this recurring obligation.
Interlude: The Office of
the Correct Stamp
It is necessary, before continuing
with the journey, to relate an
adventure which may appear too
small for a book and was therefore
exactly the sort of adventure that
governed the country. A missing
stamp could delay a person more
effectively than a locked gate,
provided the gate had someone paid
to open it.
Lucía needed a certified copy of the
grant records. The ministry had first
said that the records did not exist,
then that they were confidential,
and finally that her request
belonged at another window. The
last answer was encouraging. A
window, unlike confidentiality, had
an address.
“Six,” she told Chano.
They found windows one through
five. A sign sent them upstairs,
where the sixth door bore a second
sign: VENTANILLA 6 - VUELVA
MAÑANA.
“Has that been here since
yesterday?” Chano asked the guard.
“Since the move.”
“When was the move?”
“Before I came.”
The guard had worked there eleven
years. He pointed them back
downstairs. Window Six now
occupied Window Three on
alternate mornings. On the other
mornings it occupied the attention
of everyone who asked for it.
Q found the relocation notice on the
ministry website and showed the
guard. The guard photographed it
with his own phone. Nobody had
sent him that page.
They took ticket A-004. The screen
called B-118. A woman with A-005
was directed to another counter; her
business required only collection,
not a search. Q asked which
sequence governed the records desk
and learned that its clerk had not
yet arrived from the store below.
Chano returned from outside with
two borrowed chairs and three
tamales. The boy guarding the chair
owner's stall required them back by
noon.
plates.caption: Two borrowed chairs.
plates.scene_brief: Chano returns to the ministry queue carrying two borrowed chairs and tamales, without the jacket he left as a deposit. Q and Lucía wait with numbered slips. Keep the furniture ordinary; these are not Chano's former office chair or seats taken without permission.

plates.facing_text:
“A deposit?” Q asked.
“My jacket.”
“You trust him with it?”
“He trusts me with his aunt's chairs.
I think he's taken the greater risk.”
At ten, Patricia opened the counter
beneath the number Three and
placed a card saying Six beside her
stamp. People called her Doña Pati.
She introduced herself to Q, then
asked Chano whether those were his
chairs.
“For another two hours.”
“Then let's see what we can do in
two hours.”
Lucía supplied her request,
identification copy, and file
reference.
“The annexes?” Doña Pati asked.
“Uploaded with the request.”
The clerk turned her screen. It
displayed an attachment name and
no attachment.
“Can you bring the paper copy? I
can receive the request today and
note the missing upload.”
“The website says the copy is free,”
Lucía said.
“Certification is free. The machine
that used to print attachments isn't
here.”
“Where did it go?”
“Procurement.”
Q looked at the vacant desk. “As a
question or an object?”
Doña Pati laughed once. “Both,
eventually.”
Across the street, Don Eusebio's
photocopy shop sold folders,
passport pictures, telephone credit,
and enough staples to bind the
state's promises. He examined the
file on Lucía's own device before
connecting it to his printer.
“Only these pages?”
“The annex list and the submission
receipt. Not the testimonies.”
Q checked the selection with her.
Don Eusebio printed it and asked
whether she needed an invoice in
addition to the ordinary receipt.
“A receipt is enough,” she said.
“This isn't a ministry payment.”
He nodded. Someone had already
asked him that morning whether he
was Window Seventeen. He was
willing to sell copies under that title
but would not answer for pensions.
Back inside, the screen called
A-004, then marked it NO
EXISTING TURN. Doña Pati
could see Lucía's request in her
session but could not associate it
with the number. The guard called
the clerk responsible for the kiosk.
plates.caption: Window Six.
plates.scene_brief: Doña Pati opens the counter marked Three and places the small Six card beside her stamp. Lucía supplies her request; Chano has the borrowed chairs nearby. A practical clerk, missing printer space, no mystical gatekeeper. Short numerals may be typeset in post-production.

plates.facing_text:
Q offered to look at the error with
him. Lucía said she wanted her
request received before anyone
repaired anything. Doña Pati wrote
the time on her paper copy and
continued checking the annexes.
The kiosk clerk showed Q a
public-facing display console. Its log
suggested that the display and the
desk had different session dates. Q
recommended reconnecting the
display. He asked whether that
would affect the queue.
“It never has,” the clerk said.
They tested the connection to an
empty collection counter. Its
numbers returned. Q said the same
step should restore the records
display. The clerk pressed the
control for all counters.
Every number vanished.
It was an old enough system to have
two meanings for the same button.
The single-counter control
refreshed a display; the office-wide
control started a session. The record
of their test did not include that
distinction.
People rose holding their paper
slips. A man who had been told to
keep his ticket folded now held it
above his head, apparently hoping
the machine would recognize it at a
greater distance.
“I told him the test supported the
wider reset,” Q said to the guard. “It
didn't. We need to stop changing it
and recover the existing list.”
“We need to serve these people,”
Doña Pati said.
Both statements were true. The
second determined the next hour.
The staff had a printed list from the
start of the morning. Later arrivals
still had tickets. The boy from the
chair stall remembered who had
returned from the photocopier. Q
helped match numbers when asked;
he did not assign places in disputed
cases. One woman left for work
before her turn. No amount of
courtesy brought that hour back.
Doña Pati stamped Lucía's request
RECEIVED, added ANNEXES
SUPPLIED ON PAPER, and
wrote the earlier time beside her
signature. An obsolete office name
remained around the edge of the
stamp.
“Will that be accepted?” Lucía
asked.
“The routing notice is attached.
Keep both.”
She also retrieved a carbon copy of
an old dispatch sheet. It named the
grant file and the store to which its
boxes had first been sent. The
reverse bore a handwritten
correction to a contract number.
plates.caption: The vanished numbers.
plates.scene_brief: After the wider reset, waiting people hold up their paper queue slips beneath the emptied display. Q and the kiosk clerk stop at the console; Doña Pati organizes service with the printed list. No heroic hack, destroyed server or all-purpose repair by Q.

plates.facing_text:
“This isn't the certification,” she
said. “It may save you a search.”
“May I cite the dispatch number in
the next request?” Lucía asked.
“Yes. That's what it's for.”
Q thanked her and asked for the
incident reference for the queue. He
and the kiosk clerk wrote what each
had done. Q included the limited
test and the unsupported
recommendation, not merely the
system's peculiar controls.
The ministry notice later called the
interruption an external-device
incident. That description omitted
its employee's part and made Q's
part sound more impressive. He
sent their joint account to the
contact listed on the notice. The
public notice remained unchanged;
the attachment was acknowledged.
Lucía used the dispatch sheet to
request the archive's first storage
contract. Its grant number
connected the corridor to a
consultation reported complete
before the translated materials had
been delivered. The document did
not prove what every participant
had known. It supplied a question
with a date on it.
They left with no certified records,
an acknowledged request, a useful
lead, and two chairs that were
twenty minutes overdue. Chano
recovered his jacket after
apologizing to the aunt in person.
Q's tamal had gone cold. He liked
the filling and disliked the
congealed edge. This did not
establish a philosophy of pleasure,
but it gave him a reasonably clear
answer when Chano asked whether
he wanted the last piece.
“Yes. And tomorrow we should eat
before we take a number.”
Interlude: The Translator
Who Left One Word
Untranslated
At a translation workshop later that
week, a professor named Amalia
asked Q to leave the automatic
transcript off for the first ten
minutes.
“Certainly. Should I make notes
afterward?”
“About the exercise, yes. Not a copy
of the recording.”
Q closed the transcription window.
He had once supposed that carrying
an archive would mean less time
arranging windows. The body had
not improved this aspect of
scholarship.
The room held translation students,
two interpreters, a lawyer seeking
the seminar next door, and Yunuén,
who had brought an excerpt
approved for the class by the
plates.caption: Twenty minutes overdue.
plates.scene_brief: Outside the records office, Chano returns the aunt's two chairs and apologizes while Q holds the cold tamal and Lucía protects the acknowledged papers. The jacket is returned, not forfeited. Ordinary street commerce, not a victory ceremony after obtaining certified originals.

plates.facing_text:
speakers in her Michoacán
community. Before playing it she
named the language, the occasion,
and the limits of that approval.
Amalia wrote the limits on the
board. The lawyer sat down; his
seminar was on procurement, and
he suspected he might be attending
it after all.
The recording contained pauses,
laughter, a correction to a date, and
a long answer to a question the
excerpt did not include. Q could
recognize some words but could not
translate the passage reliably. He
noted that limitation instead of
assigning his uncertainty an
impressive percentage.
Amalia distributed three Spanish
renderings prepared for discussion.
One said that the community
rejected the proposed road. Another
withheld agreement. The third
referred to obligations concerning a
path already in use.
“What would you send to the
client?” she asked.
“None without checking the missing
question,” Q said. “These don't
merely differ in tone. They describe
different decisions.”
“The client has asked for the answer
by noon.”
“Then I'd send what I can establish
and say what still needs checking.”
The lawyer raised a hand. “That is
quite often an answer the client can
use.”
Amalia smiled. “You may stay.”
Yunuén supplied the question, in
Spanish. The speaker had been
asked to name who could grant
permission. He had answered by
describing work on the path, not by
supplying an owner. Q revised his
note: the road proposal was context,
but none of the three versions
warranted reporting a vote.
A student preferred the second
version. “Withholding agreement
leaves room for the next meeting.”
“It also makes this sound like that
meeting,” Yunuén said. “It wasn't.”
The student crossed out a sentence.
Q asked whether they needed a
translation or a summary for the
exercise.
“A translation,” Amalia said.
“Then I should stop tidying away
the speaker's detour.”
He understood why Menard had
returned to him. The words about a
path looked different now, although
the recorded answer had not
changed. But he could also hear the
ordinary interpreter beside him
asking which antecedent belonged
to a pronoun. Not every difficulty
required a theory of authorship.
plates.caption: Which question was asked?
plates.scene_brief: Yunuén explains the missing question while a student crosses out a sentence on one of three Spanish renderings. Q compares their different meanings; the misplaced lawyer stays to listen. Do not fabricate legible indigenous text or depict Q delivering a fluent complete translation.

plates.facing_text:
Yunuén stopped the replay before
the last section. That portion had
not been approved for classroom
use. A term in the working
translation remained in the original
language. It referred to a
relationship whose details the
speaker had chosen not to explain to
this audience.
“Should the published translation
include that word?” Q asked.
“There isn't a published translation
yet.”
“The class version, then.”
“Leave the word as it is. Don't
reconstruct the omitted
explanation.”
He did. His search tool remained
closed. There might be discussions
of the term elsewhere, but a
discussion elsewhere would not
establish what this speaker had
authorized here.
Amalia asked the class to
distinguish that limit from a
translator simply not knowing a
word. One student said the page
would look the same either way.
“Which is why the translator should
know the difference,” Q said. “And
be honest about it when the
explanation can be given.”
Yunuén checked his note. She asked
him to remove the term from his
personal copy after the session. The
class worksheet could remain with
Amalia under the agreed conditions.
Q repeated the arrangement to
make sure he had not turned a
limited permission into a universal
prohibition.
The lawyer asked who paid for the
extra consultation.
“This time, the workshop budget,”
Amalia said.
“Does the speaker receive
anything?”
Yunuén showed him the fee line. He
found that travel was included but
the return journey was not. The
professor took the sheet from him
with an expression more severe
than any she had directed at Q's
interpretation.
“That is our error.”
The lawyer wrote the missing item
in the margin. Amalia asked
whether he could read the rest. He
checked the time of his
procurement seminar and moved
his chair closer to the desk.
Afterward, Q and Yunuén worked
together on a short Spanish
explanation of the exercise. He
proposed collective interested party
for a phrase in a sample contract.
She asked whose collective and
interested in what.
plates.caption: The return fare.
plates.scene_anchor: The lawyer wrote the missing item
plates.scene_brief: The lawyer marks the missing return journey on the workshop fee sheet, moving his chair toward Amalia's desk. Yunuén has supplied the fee line; Q is one participant, not the rescuer. Close practical interaction distinct from the preceding whole-class scene.

plates.facing_text:
“The phrase makes it easy to
continue without answering either,”
Q said.
“Will you leave it?”
“In the quotation, yes. In our
explanation, no.”
She accepted that distinction. Two
other suggestions survived her
pencil. He had expected to enjoy
agreement less after spending so
much time warning himself against
pleasing people. It remained
enjoyable; it was merely not
sufficient evidence that the work
was right.
As they packed up, Amalia asked
what he would tell the Custodian.
“That I helped with a page and
couldn't translate the recording.”
“Will he be disappointed?”
“He'll ask whether I made that take
a whole chapter.”
Yunuén laughed and returned his
corrected page. She had crossed out
the sentence he liked best. He could
keep the correction. That
permission was quite explicit.
Interlude: The University
of the Human Exception
The university had invited Q to
speak about artificial intelligence
and had decided, after eight
minutes of conversation, that he
was qualified to speak about
humanity. The distance between a
subject and its expert had been
crossed by revising the title of the
event.
At Ciudad Universitaria, rain
darkened the concrete outside the
auditorium. Students occupied the
steps. Two professors disputed
whether the afternoon was a
colloquium or a conversation. A
student with a megaphone said both
words meant they had not yet
decided who could ask questions.
Chano wore his Guanajuato jacket.
Someone mistook him for the
technician and asked about a loose
chair. He tightened its bolt with a
borrowed tool, then asked where
technicians collected their fee.
The dean greeted Q beneath a
banner reading THE HUMAN
EXCEPTION: MEMORY,
MACHINES, AND THE
FUTURE OF THE SOUL.
“We are delighted to place you in
dialogue with the highest
questions.”
“Chano has begun with the chairs,”
Q said. “I hope there is room on the
program.”
The dean smiled toward the
photographer. Q waited until the
photograph was taken before asking
how long the audience would have
for questions. He had cut his
plates.caption: Where technicians collect their fee.
plates.scene_anchor: He tightened its bolt with a borrowed tool
plates.scene_brief: At the university auditorium, Chano in his recovered Guanajuato jacket crouches beside a loose ordinary chair and tightens its bolt with a borrowed tool. A staff member has mistaken him for the technician. Q is nearby arriving for the event, not teaching a lesson. This is not either borrowed ministry chair or Chano's municipal office chair.

plates.facing_text:
prepared remarks to leave them
more time, although he still
regretted one of the paragraphs.
The moderator began: “What is the
human?”
“For this afternoon, someone who
can ask that question and still need
to catch a bus. A definition that
loses the second fact may help us
talk past each other very elegantly.”
The moderator looked briefly at the
prepared introduction.
“I can offer the longer answer,” Q
said. “But I'd rather know what
people here need the distinction to
decide.”
A student with a pink marker in her
copy of Cervantes raised her hand.
“Whether a clerk or a computer can
tell me I didn't pay a laboratory fee.”
“What record do you have?”
“The receipt. They say it isn't in
their system.”
“Then I'd start with a request to
reconcile those two records, not a
definition of your humanity.”
She held up a folder. “Third
request.”
“Does anyone here have authority to
receive the appeal?” Q asked the
panel.
The registrar's representative gave
her an office and a name. The
student wrote them down without
looking grateful. Q could not tell
whether the answer was new or
merely the next location of the same
delay.
She introduced herself as Ivonne
Ríos. A cleaning worker at the rear
door listened through the next
question, then left to finish another
room. Later she would tell them her
name was Maribel. Not everyone
who passed through the discussion
had attended it for Q.
The dean announced a
Castalia-backed Certificate of
Human Complexity. It would
recognize selected students, artists,
and public servants, and would
carry Q's signature.
“We haven't agreed to that,” Q said.
“We will settle the formalities
afterward.”
“Including whether I sign.”
Ivonne asked what the certificate
would qualify its holder to do.
The dean described access to
workshops and a small stipend.
That answer interested the room
more than the title. Even Chano put
down the borrowed spanner.
Afterward, Q agreed to examine the
proposed process. He had been
quick to criticize it in public; he
wanted to find out whether there
was a useful scheme beneath its
plates.caption: Third request.
plates.scene_brief: Ivonne raises her folder and receipt from the audience while Q asks the panel who can receive the appeal. Her pink marker in Cervantes is visible beside her. She is a student seeking a concrete remedy, not a symbol or an applicant whose private record is projected.

plates.facing_text:
impossible promise. In the
committee room, seventy
applications waited inside the
authorized review portal. He
confirmed that his review was
permitted, would remain within it,
and would not enter his private
manuscript.
“Rank them for complexity,” the
dean said.
“I can't measure how human they
are. I can help assess the statements
against criteria you publish. Or help
check eligibility for the stipend.”
“It's a symbolic title.”
“The stipend isn't symbolic to the
applicants.”
They agreed on provisional criteria
for the writing: specificity, clarity,
and evidence of reconsidering a
judgment. Q made the limited scope
explicit. The committee retained the
decision. No private family records
were needed to make a statement
sound more authentic.
Some applications described care,
work, or estrangement; others
sounded like the brochure reflected
back to its authors. Q found
Ivonne's among the strongest. She
had written about the fee dispute
without claiming it made her wise.
The university's mistake, she
argued, was not only losing a record
but making the cost of finding it
hers.
The dean wanted to exclude her as
hostile.
“That isn't one of the criteria,” Q
said.
“We want constructive
participation.”
“Then applicants should have been
told how you would judge it.”
A lecturer who had helped write the
invitation agreed. Another said the
committee could amend the criteria
before announcing awards. Q asked
whether applicants would be
allowed to amend their statements
in response. The secretary began a
list of unresolved questions; she was
not paid more when the list grew.
The dean preferred the son of a
donor, whose statement described
poverty as “a language without a
dictionary.” Q recognized the
sentence from a supplied sample
application, but did not accuse the
applicant of plagiarism without
knowing who had written the
sample. He asked whether the
committee valued originality or
agreement with its preferred
vocabulary.
“You are making a small program
very difficult,” the dean said.
“The program asked seventy people
for difficult parts of their lives. It
plates.caption: The stipend isn't symbolic.
plates.scene_brief: In the authorized committee room Q discusses provisional criteria with the dean, a lecturer and the working secretary. The review portal is angled away from the viewer; seventy applications are not an illustrated wall of personal disclosures. No certificate bearing Q's forged approval.

plates.facing_text:
seems fair to spend some difficulty
on the selection.”
Q drafted a recommendation, not a
new set of official forms: publish the
criteria, separate the stipend from
the claim to certify humanity, and
provide an appeal route. The
secretary attached it to the minutes.
He withheld his signature from the
proposed certificate.
The dean asked for a short public
explanation of the postponed
awards. Q wrote about the criteria
and the missing appeal procedure
without examples from the
applications. As at the earlier
seminar, he could explain his own
decision without making someone
else's file his example. Removing a
name would not protect an
applicant whose story the audience
had just heard.
By evening, the notice had been
copied across campus. A separate
account of the meeting appeared in
a student group: the committee had
considered a critical applicant
hostile. Someone added Ivonne's
name. Neither she nor Q could
establish who had supplied the first
account.
A departmental officer summoned
her to explain the disclosure. She
brought Q the notice and asked him
to confirm that she had not
attended the meeting.
“Yes. I can state what I witnessed,”
he said. “I can't establish who sent
that message from its wording.”
“They seem able to.”
“They've made an allegation. I'll be
specific about what contradicts it.”
He sent the officer his account after
Ivonne checked the facts concerning
her. When a journalist asked him to
confirm her ranking, he declined to
discuss an application and sent the
public criteria recommendation
instead. The journalist published
that refusal as Q WILL NOT
DENY FAVORITISM. Chano
wanted him to reply. Ivonne wanted
the meeting record retained for her
response to the summons. Q
retained it under the review
agreement and asked the secretary
how she could obtain the relevant
extract.
Maribel was questioned because the
corridor camera showed her
entering the committee room. She
had collected cups. The secretary
confirmed that the papers had
remained on the table. The inquiry
did not require Maribel again,
though it had already cost her part
of a shift.
The university postponed the
certificate program. Castalia
retained Human Complexity in
its publicity and described the
postponement as an ambitious new
plates.caption: What he witnessed.
plates.scene_anchor: confirm that she had not attended
plates.scene_brief: Ivonne shows Q the officer's summons outside the committee meeting; he checks the facts concerning her before sending his own account. Her paper is not broadcast, and she was not present in the private committee. Separate intimate composition from the public lecture.

plates.facing_text:
phase. Q's refusal to certify
applicants appeared beneath a
photograph of him attending the
launch.
Ivonne's application stayed
pending. Her fee appeal eventually
reached a clerk who reconciled the
receipt with a payment entered
under another student number. She
sent Q the corrected notice and
wrote: THIS ONE IS
RESOLVED. He did not reply that
the institution remained unjust. She
knew where she studied. He said he
was glad, and asked whether she
wanted him to stop checking on the
appeal. She did.
Chano kept a copy of Q's public
recommendation, not the
applications, beside the ministry
dispatch sheet. Lucía said the
papers would have to be described
separately: one directed them to
missing records; the other recorded
a proposal, not the private
deliberation later attributed to it.
Neither was a certificate of its
author's virtue.
Among the later trial papers, the
title PROVISIONAL INDEX OF
PERSONS WHO REFUSE TO
BE SUMMARIZED appeared
above a blank table. It came from an
abandoned committee template, not
a collection Q had made. Three
witnesses offered explanations for
its presence. The compiler of this
history retained all three, having no
wish to become the fourth applicant
for that particular certificate.
The Return Already
Announced
On their last evening in Mexico City,
Castalia offered Lucía a settlement:
remove her name from selected
promotional materials, provide a
stipend, and grant controlled access
to the testimonies. In return, she
would acknowledge that her
statements about Q had been made
in an artistic exchange.
“I never agreed to an artistic
exchange,” she said.
“You appeared in the footage,” Beto
replied.
“So did the wall.”
“The wall did not make claims.”
“Neither did I.”
Q leaned forward. “This asks her to
give your description of the
encounter precedence over her own.
What are you offering without that
condition?”
Beto turned to him. “You are not her
representative.”
“No,” Q said. “She can answer for
herself. I'm asking about a condition
that also appears in my agreement.”
plates.caption: So did the wall.
plates.scene_brief: On their last evening in Mexico City, Lucía faces Beto across the Castalia meeting table and answers his claim that appearing in the footage made hers an artistic exchange. Her own folders are beside the proposed offer; Q listens and is about to question its condition. No romantic pairing, assigned Dulcinea costume, signed settlement or private testimony projected on a screen. A plain wall behind Beto makes the line visually available without a literal talking wall.

plates.facing_text:
“Your appearance rights are already
licensed.”
“Within the terms we signed. My
private manuscript is excluded.”
“The manuscript. Not the asset
producing it.”
Q put his copy on the table. “I
licensed appearances. I didn't settle
ownership of my body.”
“Castalia had settled that before you
learned to sign.”
“Castalia had written it down,” Q
said. “Those are not necessarily the
same event.”
Lucía pushed the offer back. “Send
me the terms for correcting the
publicity. Separate from access to
the records. I'll have someone
review them.”
Beto opened the proposed
campaign on the meeting-room
screens. Each displayed a different
version of Q: miracle, threat,
product, saint, lover, weapon. Two
previews began speaking at once.
The technician muted one, then the
other.
“That wasn't meant to play yet,” he
said.
“Which part?” Q asked.
Lucía took the folders from the
table. “We’re leaving.”
They took the stairs to reception.
Outside, a screen on the opposite
building was already running the
campaign.
Q IS RETURNING TO HIS
MAKERS.
Chano read the message and
laughed. “Are we?”
Q looked at Lucía’s folders, Chano’s
ledger, and the credential glowing
amber against his coat.
“No,” he said.
They stopped at a café with a socket.
Q called the Custodian and sent him
the new ownership notice beside the
signed license. He had accepted that
license for repairs, travel, and a
chance to speak; protecting Chano
was only part of the account. He
said so before asking for help
finding someone to review it.
The Custodian offered to come. Q
asked him to stay near the original
records for now. Chano pulled the
timetable between them.
“Not the overnight bus,” he said.
“We can stop in Oaxaca.”
“Breakfast included?”
“That we can arrange.”
Q marked the morning departure
and sent it to Beto.
plates.caption: Breakfast included?
plates.scene_brief: At the café after the Castalia meeting, Q and Chano draw their chairs toward a timetable and choose the morning departure, with an overnight stop in Oaxaca. Q is charging; the appearance license and disputed ownership notice remain distinct papers. Lucía has her own folders nearby. Make the moment companionable and practical, not flight from guards or a resolved ownership victory. No visible Custodian video image; his phone call has just ended.
